analysis.one_liner: Closes Clean Air Act loopholes so oil and gas emissions are counted together for air-toxics rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add hydrogen sulfide, a toxic gas released by oil and gas operations, to the official list of hazardous air pollutants. It would also repeal special loopholes written into the Clean Air Act that bar the EPA from adding up emissions from a company's nearby oil and gas wells, pumps, and compressors to determine whether they count as a 'major source' of toxic air pollution, and bar the EPA from even listing oil and gas production wells as a category it regulates. Without aggregation, many polluting facilities stay below the thresholds that trigger federal air-toxics controls. The bill was referred to committee and never advanced [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near oil and gas wells, compressor stations, and pipelines, especially in areas with many wells clustered together. These facilities emit hazardous pollutants including hydrogen sulfide, and the bill would have made them count together for federal air-toxics standards [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near oil and gas wells

how_it_helps.text: Adds hydrogen sulfide to the list of hazardous air pollutants regulated under the Clean Air Act's air-toxics program [S2][S3].

Repeals the statutory prohibition on aggregating emissions from oil and gas wells and pipeline compressor or pump stations, so combined emissions can determine whether a site is a major source subject to hazardous air pollutant standards [S2][S3].

Repeals the prohibition on aggregating emissions from oil and gas wells for any hazardous air pollutant standard, and restores the EPA's authority to list oil and gas production wells as an area source category of hazardous air pollutants [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas exploration and production companies, which could face stricter federal air-toxics controls on wells, compressor stations, and pump stations once their emissions are counted together, with some of those costs passed through in energy prices [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Aggregating emissions could reclassify many previously small, individually permitted wells as part of a major source, subjecting small and mid-sized producers to the major-source permitting and control regime of the Clean Air Act [S2][S3].

Listing hydrogen sulfide as a hazardous air pollutant would extend air-toxics requirements to oil and gas and related facilities handling the gas, a cost supporters would have to weigh against the public-health benefit [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is targeted: stronger federal air-toxics enforcement matters most in areas where many wells and compressor stations are clustered near homes. The cost is borne by oil and gas operators, and how much reaches consumers depends on how controls are implemented. The bill was narrow enough that it would not broadly rewrite oil and gas regulation, but it also never received committee scrutiny, so the practical cost figures were never tested in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Polis introduced the bill on March 17, 2011, joined by eight original cosponsors, all House Democrats [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and on March 28, 2011, referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
The bill gathered 24 Democratic cosponsors but no Republican ones [S4].
No further action was recorded after the subcommittee referral; the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill still in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers are better off: they continue to operate under the aggregation exemption and the exclusion of hydrogen sulfide from the hazardous air pollutants list, and communities near wells received no new federal air-toxics protection [S2][S3].

for.name: Rep. Jared Polis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or reported it out; the bill died in committee after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and none were Republicans, though no floor vote ever tested party lines [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have removed Clean Air Act exemptions letting their emissions be treated well-by-well rather than aggregated, which could trigger major-source air-toxics controls on clustered wells, compressor stations, and pump stations. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs against the interest of nearby residents in cleaner air [S2][S3].
